title: WAL — Write-Ahead Log
description: Master write-ahead logging for durability: redo vs undo logging, checkpoint tuning, group commit optimization, and PostgreSQL WAL configuration for production.

segments.text: Every serious database uses a write-ahead log. The principle is simple but powerful: before modifying any data page, write the intended change to a sequential log. If the system crashes, replay the log to recover. WAL is the foundation of database durability, and tuning it correctly can 10x your write throughput.

Why not just write data directly? Because data pages are scattered randomly across disk. Writing to page 5, then page 5000, then page 12 means random I/O. The WAL converts random writes into sequential appends. Sequential writes on an HDD are 100 times faster than random writes. Even on SSDs, sequential writes reduce write amplification.

Redo logging records the new values: set page 42, offset 100, to value X. After a crash, scan the log forward and apply all committed changes. This is what PostgreSQL uses. The advantage: you can write dirty pages to disk lazily because the WAL has all the information needed to reconstruct any committed transaction.

Undo logging records the old values: page 42 previously had value Y. After a crash, scan the log backward and undo any uncommitted changes. InnoDB uses a combination: redo log for committed transactions, undo log for rollbacks and MVCC. This dual approach supports both recovery and concurrent reads of old versions.

When a transaction commits, the WAL record must be flushed to disk before the commit returns. This fsync is the bottleneck for write-heavy workloads. If you're doing 10,000 transactions per second and each fsync takes 0.5 milliseconds, that's 5 seconds of fsync time per second. How do you solve this impossibility?
segments.thought_prompt: How can a database commit 10,000 transactions per second if each fsync takes 0.5ms?

segments.text: Group commit is the answer. Instead of fsyncing after every transaction, batch multiple commits into a single fsync. PostgreSQL collects all pending commits during a configurable window, typically one to ten milliseconds, and flushes them together. One fsync for 50 transactions instead of 50 fsyncs. This is the single biggest WAL optimization.

Without checkpoints, crash recovery would replay the entire WAL from the beginning of time. Checkpoints flush all dirty pages to disk and write a checkpoint record to the WAL. Recovery only needs to replay from the last checkpoint. PostgreSQL triggers checkpoints every five minutes or when WAL reaches max_wal_size, default one gigabyte.

Checkpoint tuning is critical. A checkpoint that flushes too much data at once causes an I/O spike that degrades query performance. PostgreSQL's checkpoint_completion_target spreads the I/O over the checkpoint interval. Set it to 0.9 to use 90 percent of the interval for spreading writes. This eliminates the sawtooth latency pattern during checkpoints.

Key PostgreSQL WAL settings. wal_buffers: shared memory for WAL records before flushing, default 16 megabytes. synchronous_commit on means guaranteed durability. Setting it to off gives 2 to 3x more write throughput but risks losing the last 200 milliseconds of transactions on crash. Some teams use off for analytics, on for payments.

WAL isn't just for crash recovery. Streaming replication sends WAL records to replica servers in real time. The replica applies them to stay in sync. This is how PostgreSQL read replicas work. The WAL becomes a replication protocol. Replication lag is the delay between WAL generation on the primary and application on the replica.

Here's a production tradeoff that causes heated debate. A payments team wants synchronous replication to prevent data loss. The replica is in another availability zone with two-millisecond network latency. Every commit now takes at least two milliseconds longer. Write throughput drops 60 percent. Is the durability worth the performance cost?
segments.thought_prompt: For a payment system, would you accept 60% throughput reduction for zero data loss on failover?

segments.text: The WAL is the most important data structure in any database. It converts random writes to sequential writes, enables crash recovery, powers replication, and supports point-in-time recovery. Tune group commit for throughput, spread checkpoints for latency, and choose your synchronous_commit setting based on your durability requirements.
